In the D study, these components are combined into reliability coefficients for a specific measurement design, that is, for ratings averaged across a given number of conditions per facet. The generalizability coefficient Eρ 2 quantifies how consistently the relative ordering of the stimuli is reproduced across facet conditions, whereas the dependability coefficient Φ additionally takes differences in the absolute level of the ratings into account.

Because a D study can be computed for any number of conditions per facet, researchers can also project how reliability will change if different numbers of models, prompt variants, or iterations are used. When planning the analysis, researchers should specify the mixed model, which facets are treated as random or fixed, how the universe score is defined, which coefficient is of primary interest, and which D study designs will be evaluated. The case study below illustrates these steps in detail.

Importantly, high consistency across simulation conditions does not imply that the output is correct or valid. High estimates of consistency can also emerge if LLMs systematically give incorrect or biased responses. Therefore, the weak validation criterion is not sufficient by itself to judge the quality of LLM ratings. Still, the approach is useful as a first step to identify methodological factors that shape LLM response distributions when an external criterion is not (yet) available.

If an external criterion is available for comparison (e.g., human ratings), the inter-rater reliability between human ratings and LLM ratings may be computed as the Pearson or rank-order correlation of ratings across all stimulus materials (Goodwin, 2001).

The choice between measures of relative and absolute agreement should follow from the intended use of the LLM ratings. The distinction between relative and absolute agreement parallels the generalizability and dependability coefficients in generalizability theory, which concern the relative ordering and the absolute level of ratings, respectively (Brennan, 2001).

Measures of relative agreement (e.g., Pearson or rank-order correlations, or the consistency intraclass correlation ICC(C,1); McGraw and Wong, 1996) are sufficient when LLM ratings are used to order stimuli, to select stimuli covering the range of a construct, or as covariates or predictors in statistical models, since these uses are unaffected by linear transformations of the ratings. Measures of absolute agreement (e.g., mean bias, root mean square error across items, or the agreement intraclass correlation ICC(A,1)) are required whenever the generated values themselves are interpreted, for instance, when LLM ratings are combined with existing human norms, when stimuli are selected based on cutoff values (e.g., to select "neutral" items), or when LLMs are used to predict or forecast observable quantities such as voting behavior (von der Heyde et al., 2025).

Because high correlations do not preclude systematic shifts or a compressed range of LLM ratings (Abdurahman et al., 2024), researchers may additionally compare the distributions of LLM and human ratings (e.g., means and standard deviations).

For any measure, one should specify whether LLM ratings are averaged across prompt iterations before computing the mean across items. Furthermore, researchers may employ a rater non-inferiority criterion, demanding that the agreement between LLM and human ratings should be as high as the agreement between different human raters (Cummins et al., 2026). If a study targets specific comparisons between LLM configurations (e.g., whether a smaller local model agrees with human ratings as well as a commercial model), these comparisons can be tested statistically. Because both correlations share the same benchmark ratings, they are dependent, and tests for independent correlations are not appropriate. Suitable tests and confidence intervals for dependent correlations are implemented, for instance, in the R package cocor (Diedenhofen & Musch, 2015). Such targeted tests are most informative when the comparisons are specified in advance; in exploratory multiverse designs, the number of possible pairwise comparisons grows quickly, so that summarizing the overall pattern (e.g., by variance components or plots of all conditions) is often more useful than testing every pair. Researchers may be interested in computing logprobs of token predictions to obtain probability-weighted expected ratings that reflect the uncertainty associated with each token (e.g., Hussain et al., 2024; Martínez et al., 2024).

The estimation uncertainty of some performance measures (such as the correlation of LLM and human ratings) is bounded by the number n items of stimulus items included in the study. The sampling error due to having a finite number of items is relevant with respect to generalizing the results to other items from the target domain (Brennan, 2010).

To assess this type of uncertainty, we can average the standard error of an agreement measure across simulation iterations (e.g., the mean SE of the correlation coefficient).

Importantly, the averaged standard error depends on the number of items and does not automatically decrease even if more conditions or iterations are used.

A different source of uncertainty in LLM simulations is due to the stochasticity of repeated LLM ratings within the same condition (Knöchel et al., 2025). This uncertainty can be reported in the form of the Monte Carlo standard error (MCSE) and decreases for a larger number of iterations. When studying the quality of LLM-generated ratings, we consider the MCSE to be less relevant than the uncertainty due to studying only a limited number of items, since it depends on a property of the specific procedure (i.e., how many repeated LLM ratings were elicited) and not a property of the content (i.e., whether the rating methodology generalized across the item domain). LLM output can deviate from the allowed range of responses, resulting in invalid or missing values. If ratings are to be confined to numerical values in a bounded, predefined range (e.g., Likert ratings between 1 and 7), provide information on how other output (e.g., non-numeric text or values outside of the range) will be treated. One possibility is to handle these values as missing data and report their relative occurrence rate. To reduce such issues, researchers can use LLM software that ensures a certain output structure, for instance, by specifying a specific JSON template (for example with software packages such as ellmer in R; Wickham et al., 2025). If such methods are not used, it may be the case that the rating of interest is still included in the open text output and can potentially be retrieved by further text processing. If this is the case, describe the steps taken to extract relevant information from the open text format. As an alternative to treating invalid responses as missings, it is possible to impute iterations that did not return a valid rating, for instance, by implementing repeated prompting until a valid output rating is obtained (for different strategies of handling missingness in simulations, see Pawel et al., 2026). Furthermore, specify at which proportion of failed iterations a whole condition will be excluded from the analysis.

Finally, one may specify thresholds to reduce post-hoc flexibility in interpreting the results. For example, one could specify what will constitute 'acceptable' and 'unacceptable' levels of performance and what will count as 'relevant differences' in the performance of different LLMs. Still, any verbal labels should be interpreted cautiously, especially if they are based on arbitrary conventions.

Other Information

The last section of the template documents the employed software versions and the computational environment used for the LLM simulation. List the primary packages intended for LLM usage, including their version number. Additionally, include information about the operating system that will be used for running all analyses and for hosting the LLMs. If different computers or servers are utilized for the LLM simulation and the subsequent analysis, report information regarding each of these environments.

After the analysis, the code employed to execute all analyses, as well as the intermediate or complete results of the analyses should be stored in an open online repository. Supplemental materials may also be provided to ensure a comprehensive documentation of the employed methodology (Argyle et al., 2025). This section can also include information about the most likely obstacles in LLM prompting (e.g., issues with the API or LLM service due to repeated requests) or the simulation design, and plans to overcome them.

Case Study: Evaluating the Quality of LLM Ratings for Valence and Arousal

As a case study, we present a preregistered application of the modified ADEMP and 5 validated GPT-4o ratings of valence and arousal, respectively, against human ratings for two different sets of 96 multi-word expressions, yielding correlations of r = .95 (valence) and r = .92 (arousal).

We conducted two separate LLM simulation studies-one for valence and one for arousal-since ratings for the two constructs were validated using different item sets. In each simulation, we varied the choice of LLM and the prompt structure by manipulating the required response format and the type of prompt examples provided as context.

Assessing both consistency and inter-rater reliability, our analyses focused on the variance decomposition of LLM-generated ratings and the correlation of LLM and human ratings of valence and arousal provided by Martínez et al. (2024).

Before conducting the reported simulation study, we ran preliminary tests to assess the usefulness of the modified ADEMP template and ascertain the functionality of the analysis pipeline. For this purpose, we evaluated the quality of LLM ratings regarding the syntactic complexity of factual statements using the items and human ratings by Schmidt and Heck (2024). The code for this pilot study is available on Zenodo (https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23810473).

Preregistered Evaluation of LLM-Generated Valence and Arousal Ratings

We used the ADEMP template for LLM simulation studies for planning and preregistration (https://osf.io/8e6gf). 3 We report the results for valence in the main text and those for arousal in the supplementary materials (https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23810473).

Aims

The aims of the LLM simulation study are (1) to conduct a variance decomposition of LLM ratings of valence and arousal regarding multi-word expressions into construct variance (due to differences in the valence and arousal of the included items) and method variance (due to specific LLM and prompt variations) and ( 2) to assess the extent to which LLM ratings correspond to the perceived valence and arousal of multi-word expressions as rated by humans.

Data-Generating Mechanism

Our study uses two different sets of English multi-word expressions (each with n items = 96 items). Martínez et al. (2024) selected the stimuli based on their own GPT-4o ratings to cover the entire range of the respective construct. In Experiments 4 and 5, human raters rated the stimuli regarding valence and arousal, respectively. All analyses were conducted separately for the multi-word expressions of valence and arousal but with identical methodology reported in the Methods section. All LLM calls were independent by starting each LLM call with a fresh context (also see Conde et al., 2026).

We used open-weights LLMs which are run locally through the software Ollama (Ollama, 2026) and are accessed via the R package ellmer. To ensure that LLM ratings of valence and arousal only consist of numerical values, we used the type_object() and type_integer() functions to request output in JSON format with a predetermined response format of integers. Each prompt is composed according to the structure used by Martínez et al. (2024) in prompt 2 (valence) and prompt 3 (arousal) of their paper: (1)

An explanation of the task, (2) the range of responses allowed, (3) examples for multi-word expressions, (4) the target multi-word expression to be rated, and (5) a reminder for the range of responses allowed.

Estimands and Targets

Our target estimands are the valence and arousal of multi-word expressions (where the scale varies across conditions as detailed in the Methods section in the following). Valence and arousal are the two primary variables of dimensional models of affect (Russell, 1980). Valence refers to the pleasantness of a stimulus, ranging from very negative to very positive, whereas arousal refers to the intensity of the emotional activation elicited by a stimulus, ranging from calm to excited (Warriner et al., 2013).

Methods

We included eight open-weights models by four companies that can efficiently be run locally using

Ollama on a GPU with 32GB VRAM without requiring access to an online service. The eight models were gemma3 (with 4b, 12b, and 27b parameters; Google)foot_3 , llama3.1 (8b parameters; Meta), phi3 (3.8b, 14b parameters; Microsoft), phi4 (14b parameters; Microsoft), and gpt-oss (20b parameters; OpenAI). All model parameters were kept at the values that applied by default in our software setup. We deliberately did not tune these settings, because default configurations correspond to how most researchers will use these models in practice, which makes the results informative for typical applications. Although Ollama documents a default temperature of 0.8 for models without a model-specific value (llama3.1:8b, phi3:3.8b, phi3:14b, phi4:14b), accessing Ollama via ellmer sets temperature and top-p to 1 for all requests.

Hence, all eight models ran with the same temperature and top-p, whereas top-k was 64 for the gemma3 models and 40 for all other models. Appendix B documents all settings, and an additional check in the supplementary materials confirmed empirically that ratings obtained with the default settings corresponded to those obtained with a temperature of 1 rather than 0.8. All models were updated to their most recent version at 28/01/2026.

We adopted the prompt design by Martínez et al. (2024) to obtain either a valence or an arousal rating while manipulating two key components in a fully factorial setting: (1) The format of the rating task (a 1-9 or a 0-100 scale) and ( 2) The presence and type of example expressions provided: no example expressions; three examples for low valence or arousal (lower anchor); three examples for high valence or arousal (upper anchor); or three examples for both low and high valence or arousal (both lower and upper anchor).

The last condition corresponds to the original prompt design used by Martínez et al. (2024). Ratings of valence and arousal were obtained in two separate and independent steps of the LLM simulation. The system prompt was empty, thus not providing any custom system instructions. Example prompts can be found in the Appendix.

The complete LLM simulation design including all investigated method factors had 8 × 2 ×4 = 64 distinct conditions in total, as summarized by the following list: • Model: eight models from four different companies, run locally using Ollama • Format: response scale, ranging either from 1 to 9 or from 0 to 100, that the LLMs had to adhere to in their response • Example: four types of different examples provided to the LLMs (none, lower anchor, upper anchor, both lower and upper anchor)

Performance Measures

The present investigation used two performance measures: (1) Estimating the variance components in LLM-generated valence and arousal ratings associated with differences in the stimulus materials and differences in methods (secondary performance measure focusing on consistency), and (2) assessing the correlation between human and LLM ratings of valence and arousal (primary performance measure focusing on inter-rater reliability).

Regarding aim (1), we estimated the variance components of the following linear mixed model using the gtheory package (Moore, 2016) which uses the lmer() function, lmer(llm_rating ~(1 | stimulus * model * format * example),... )

The stimulus term accounts for differences in the target construct between the multi-word expressions (i.e., actual variability in valence or arousal), whereas the remaining terms (model, format, and example) account for methods effects.

Following generalizability theory, we first performed a G study, in which the variance components of all random effects (main effects and interactions) were estimated from the fitted model and expressed as percentages of their sum (Brennan, 2001). All variance components were estimated as random effects because each model, example type, and response format is drawn from a potentially infinite universe with the stimuli being the object of measurement. The realization of the chosen model, exact example type, and presentation of the response format are to some extent arbitrary and interchangeable and could differ across studies. Treating any of these facets as fixed would move interactions of the stimuli with these facets to the universe score variance and thereby increase the generalizability and dependability coefficients. The present analysis can therefore be regarded as conservative.

In the D study, the universe score of a stimulus is its expected rating across all admissible conditions of the facets (e.g., across all models and prompt variants that could have been used), and the variance of these scores across stimuli constitutes the universe score variance. We defined it as σ 2 (τ ) = σ 2 (stimulus) (i.e., as the true, unknown random-intercept variance of the stimuli), because we aimed to evaluate how well the obtained stimulus LLM ratings generalize across the investigated facets of the design (8 models, 4 example conditions, 2 response formats). The generalizability coefficient compares the universe score variance to the relative error variance σ 2 (δ), which comprises all components involving an interaction with the stimuli and thus affects the relative ordering of stimulus ratings.

In contrast, the dependability coefficient is based on the absolute error variance σ 2 (∆), which additionally includes facet main effects and their interactions, so that Φ ≤ Eρ 2 .

Our analysis focuses on Eρ 2 , as our study focuses on whether LLMs can produce stimulus ratings that show the same relative ordering (but not necessarily the exact same values) as those provided by humans.

The D study variance components were obtained by dividing the respective G study variance components by the product of the number of factor levels per involved facet (excluding the object of measurement -the stimuli). For example, the D study variance component for the interaction of the stimulus s, the model facet m, and the example facet e is given by σ 2 (sM E) = σ 2 (sme) , where σ 2 (sme) is the corresponding G study variance component and n ′ m and n ′ e are the number of models (= 8) and example conditions (= 4), respectively.

The capital letters M and E indicate that the estimated variance component is for stimulus mean scores across 8 models and 4 example type conditions. Because σ 2 (sM E) involves an interaction with the stimuli, it is part of σ 2 (δ), whereas components without such an interaction (e.g., σ 2 (M E)) enter only the absolute error variance σ 2 (∆).

Regarding aim (2) about the agreement between human and LLM ratings, we computed the Pearson correlation coefficient,

We focused on relative agreement because the case study aimed to identify method factors affecting the relative ordering of stimulus ratings, which is the relevant property when LLM-generated norms are used to order or select stimuli and which corresponds to the validation strategy of Martínez et al. (2024). Moreover, absolute agreement would be partly arbitrary, since ratings from the two response formats (1-9 and 0-100) would first have to be rescaled to the human rating scale. We computed the correlation at two different levels of the analysis: • (a) At the level of individual iterations in each simulation condition, we computed the correlation between human ratings and LLM ratings across expressions.

The inter-rater reliability (IRR) was estimated by the average correlation,

To assess the estimation error due to the finite number of iterations, we computed the Monte Carlo standard error, where is the sample standard deviation of the estimate and n sim is the number of simulation iterations (see Siepe et al., 2024).

• (b) At the level of aggregated LLM ratings (averaged across all simulation iterations within each simulation condition), we computed the correlation between human and LLM ratings. Using a bootstrap procedure, n est LLM ratings were first randomly drawn with replacement from the n sim iterations of a simulation condition for each stimulus and then aggregated into an average rating. These average ratings per stimulus were then used to compute the inter-rater reliability between human-generated and LLM-generated ratings. This procedure was repeated n sim times to ensure that the same number of estimates was obtained as when using raw LLM ratings.

To quantify uncertainty due to the limited number of items, we averaged the standard errors of the correlations for the n items = 96 expressions across iterationsfoot_4 ; to quantify uncertainty due to the limited number of iterations, we computed MCSEs (Siepe et al., 2024). Both types of standard errors and corresponding 95% CIs are reported in plots and as tables in the online materials.

We performed 100 simulation iterations per condition. The number of iterations was determined based on preliminary testing with ratings of syntactic complexity (Schmidt & Heck, 2024), which showed that this number of iterations resulted in narrow MCSE 95% confidence intervals while ensuring computational feasibility. LLM ratings that did not fall within the specified range of admissible rating values (integers either between 1 to 9 or between 0 to 100 depending on the condition) were treated as missing values. We report the proportion of such cases and excluded conditions if the proportion of missing values exceeded 20% based on a rule of thumb.

Regarding our primary performance measure, the correlation between human and LLM ratings, we preregistered the following thresholds: an inter-rater reliability of IRR ≥ .70 was labeled acceptable, IRR ≥ .80 adequate, and IRR ≥ .90 (as obtained with GPT-4o by Martínez et al., 2024) excellent. These cutoffs follow common conventions for reliability coefficients, which were proposed mainly in the context of test-retest reliability (Groh, 2025; Matheson, 2019). The specific cutoffs and their verbal labels should therefore not be read as substantive quality categories, but rather serve to constrain post-hoc flexibility in interpreting the results. The continuous estimates and their uncertainty remain the primary basis for interpretation. We considered a certain method as performing better (or worse) than these thresholds on the employed corpus if the MCSE 95% CI was above (below) a threshold. We considered Method X as performing better than Method Y in a certain simulation condition on the employed corpus if the lower bound for the estimated inter-rater reliability of Method X ( IRR -1.96 • MCSE) was greater than the upper bound for the estimated inter-rater reliability of Method Y ( IRR + 1.96 • MCSE). Conversely, if the 95% CI based on the averaged standard errors of correlation coefficients between human-generated and LLM-generated ratings was above (below) one of the thresholds, we concluded that a certain method is generally better (worse) than this threshold for comparable stimulus material. As noted above, the MCSE-based CI only reflects the precision of the estimate in a condition, not whether performance generalizes to new stimuli.

Other Information

We used R version 4.5.2 (R Core Team, 2025) for the LLM simulation and the R package ellmer 0.4.0 (Wickham et al., 2025) for standardizing the API calls to the locally installed LLMs, which were run via Ollama 0.12.9 (https://ollama.com/; Ollama, 2026). We ran the LLM simulation study on a Kubuntu 24.04 machine using an Nvidia GPU (RTX 5090) with CUDA 13.0. For the analyses based on the obtained LLM simulation results, we used R version 4.6.0 and the following R packages in their most recent versions: tidyverse 2.0.0 (Wickham et al., 2019) and ggplot2 4.0.3 (Wickham, 2016) packages for data analysis and visualization, papaja 0.1.4 for modification of plots according to APA guidelines (Aust & Barth, 2025), and gtheory 0.1.2 (Moore, 2016) and lme4 2.0-1 (Bates et al., 2015) for conducting generalizability theory analyses. The complete output of sessionInfo for all analyses is available at Zenodo (computational_environment.txt; https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23810473). The fully reproducible simulation script and a data set containing all LLM ratings of valence and arousal as well as the correlation between LLM ratings and human ratings with their confidence intervals are available at Zenodo (https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23810473). Furthermore, we generated random seeds for each of the LLM ratings prior to the simulation, thereby ensuring the reproducibility of our analysis. 6

Transparency and Openness

We report how we determined our sample size, all data exclusions, all manipulations, and all measures in the study, and we follow JARS (Appelbaum et al., 2018). All data, analysis code, and research materials are available at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23810473. This study's design and its initial analysis were preregistered; see https://osf.io/8e6gf/overview. Upon revision of the manuscript and following reviewer comments, we preregistered additional analyses and replaced the fixed-effects variance decomposition with a generalizability theory analysis under https://osf.io/28ja9/. We used Claude Sonnet 4.6 and Opus 5.5 (Anthropic, 2026) and DeepL Write (DeepL, 2026) for grammar checking and linguistic revision and reviewed all proposed changes.

Results for Valence Ratings

Missing Values

Of the 614,400 LLM ratings (64 conditions × 96 expressions × 100 iterations), 38 were missing due to internal errors returned by Ollama during prompt processing (gpt-oss 6 While testing to see if we would obtain the same LLM ratings for multi-word expressions by repeating a prompt with the same seed, we found that calls to gpt-oss (20b) did not always produce the same output.

Variance Decomposition by Method Factors

To address aim (1), we first rescaled ratings from the 1-9 format to the 0-100 scale to avoid artificial differences between response formats and then fitted the mixed model specified above. Table 1 shows the estimated variance components and their percentages. Since we aimed to investigate consistency-whether the ordering of stimuli was stable across models, response formats, and prompt examples-we were predominantly interested in the interactions involving the stimulus factor, that is, the relative error variance components. For instance, a stimulus × model interaction would indicate that item ratings vary systematically between LLMs.

The stimulus factor accounted for the by far largest proportion of variance (68.85%) in LLM valence ratings. This is desirable, as actual differences in the valence of multi-word expressions perceived by humans (i.e., the construct variance, or universe score variance in generalizability theory, to be measured) should have the largest effect on LLM ratings. Still, Table 1 shows that a considerable portion of the observed variance (almost 20%) was attributable to methodological facets (method variance). The residual variance component (12.84%) was relatively small, indicating limited variability of ratings across iterations within each cell of the design. 7In the D study, we estimated the coefficients Eρ 2 and Φ for our design with eight model conditions, four example conditions, and two response format conditions. The generalizability coefficient Eρ2 = .98 corresponds to the expected correlation between mean ratings from two independent studies with different facet conditions (Brennan, 2001), indicating excellent reliability. The dependability coefficient was only slightly lower (Φ = .96), indicating that absolute valence ratings for the stimuli (averaged across facets) were reliable. The D study above assumes a single iteration per cell. Beyond the analyses we preregistered, we considered the number of iterations in an additional analysis for another D study, leading to a shrinkage of the residual term, resulting in Eρ2 = .99 and Φ = .97. Given the already high coefficients, accounting for the 100 iterations led to only marginal improvements here, although averaging across iterations generally reduces error variance in LLM simulations (see also the aggregation analysis below). Finally, we conducted another exploratory D study where the number of facets per factor was set to n = 1, yielding Eρ2 = .75, indicating the expected correlation between two different LLM-rating conditions across the investigated stimuli (moreover, Φ = .69).

Similar results were obtained for LLM arousal ratings. However, the proportion of variance reflecting universe score variance of stimulus ratings (52.53%) was substantially lower compared to that of valence ratings (68.85%), indicating lower consistency. The effect of this difference was especially apparent when the number of facets was set to n = 1 where Eρ2 = .75 for ratings of valence but Eρ2 = .58 for ratings of arousal, indicating that ratings of arousal from a single measurement procedure are not as reliable. we retained the full model rather than simplifying it as described in the preregistration for convergence problems.

Correlation Between Human and LLM Ratings

To address aim (2), we computed the correlation between human and LLM valence ratings across the 96 stimuli for each of the 64 conditions (Figure 2; the dashed line indicates the correlation of r = .95 obtained with GPT-4o by Martínez et al., 2024).

As correlations are bounded by the reliability of the variables, we also assessed the reliability of the human benchmark ratings with an analogous generalizability analysis. In the G study, a crossed design with random intercepts for stimuli, raters, and their interaction (the residual) attributed 59.66%, 0.76%, and 39.58% of the variance in human ratings to these components, respectively. In the D study, the generalizability coefficient (cf. Equation 1) was computed as, where σ 2 (sr) is the stimulus-by-rater (residual) component and n ′ r the number of raters.

The resulting Eρ2 = .96 (arousal: .95, based on 23 raters) indicates excellent reliability of the mean valence ratings across the 16 raters in Martínez et al. (2024), meaning that the mean item ratings from two independent sets of 16 raters would be expected to correlate at r = .96. In this simple crossed design, Eρ 2 is equivalent to Cronbach's α computed across persons instead of items (Brennan, 2001). In contrast, the averaged 95% confidence intervals (gray shaded areas), which reflect the limited number of 96 stimuli, were considerably wider. However, even accounting for the limited number of items, it is evident that the models differed in their ability to approximate human ratings of multi-word expressions.

Figure 2 shows that the models gemma3 (27b parameters) and gpt-oss (20b parameters) achieved an excellent, albeit slightly lower correlation with human ratings in most conditions compared to the results for GPT-4o reported by Martínez et al. (2024, IRR ≥ .90). Some models such as llama3.1 (8b parameters) and phi3 (3.8b parameters) achieved acceptable correlations with human ratings ( IRR ≥ .70) in some conditions but showed greater dependence on the specific simulation condition. The highest correlation of r = .92 between human and LLM ratings was achieved by gpt-oss (20b parameters) using a 1-9 response scale with only high-valence examples in the prompt. Figure 3 provides a scatterplot of human ratings and mean LLM ratings averaged across iterations for each stimulus and simulation condition for the best-performing model. Note that averaging across all iterations before computing the correlation between human and LLM ratings increases the correlation to r = .95. Regarding LLM ratings for arousal, we observed similar, but on average lower correlations of up to r ≈ .80 ("adequate performance"), below the performance of r = .92 observed by Martínez et al. (2024) for GPT-4o.

To assess whether the performance ranking of LLM simulation conditions generalizes to new stimuli, we conducted a split-half analysis (exploratory). We randomly split the 96 stimuli into two halves of 48 stimuli each. Within each half, we computed the correlation between human and LLM ratings for each condition and iteration and averaged these correlations across iterations, yielding 64 average correlations per half (one per condition). We then computed the Pearson and Spearman correlations between the two halves across the 64 conditions. Repeating this procedure for 1,000 random splits yielded a mean split-half correlation of r = .95 [.90, .98] and a mean rank correlation of r s = .90 [.83, .95] (values within square brackets indicate 95% percentiles). Applying the Spearman-Brown formula to estimate the stability for the full set of 96 stimuli yielded r = .97 and r s = .95. Thus, the relative performance of the LLM simulation conditions was highly stable across independent sets of stimuli. However, this stability does not guarantee that the findings generalize to new datasets (see next section).

We further assessed whether the ordering of the 64 conditions in terms of their correlation with human ratings generalizes from valence to arousal (Figure 4). Conditions with higher correlations for valence also tended to show higher correlations for arousal, r = .68, p < .001 (r s = .58, p < .001). As Figure 4 suggests, this consistency was mostly

Discussion

The present work proposes a systematic workflow for evaluating the quality of LLM-generated ratings for stimulus materials. We take a novel perspective by connecting LLM-based methodology for natural language processing with traditional methodological simulation studies. Our framework enhances the coherence across disparate fields that have used LLMs to elicit ratings and promotes the adoption of rigorous methodological standards that have been effective in related disciplines. To this end, we adapted the ADEMP framework originally proposed in the field of statistics for simulation studies (Morris et al., 2019) and the corresponding ADEMP-PreReg template (Siepe et al., 2024).

Given the inherent flexibility and numerous, often arbitrary design choices 1 5 10 25 50100 1 5 10 25 50100 1 5 10 25 50100 1 5 10 25 50100 1 5 10 25 50100 1 5 10 25 50100 1 5 10 25 50100 1 5 10 25 50100 0.50 0.60 0.70 0.80 0.90 1.00 n est correlation between human and LLM ratings Note. The plot shows the condition with both types of examples and a 1-9 scale. The dashed, horizontal line indicates the correlation between human and LLM ratings obtained with GPT-4o by Martínez et al. (2024). Colored error bars (dark gray in print) indicate 95% confidence bounds based on the MCSE.

involved in generating LLM ratings, a simulation-based multiverse analysis that quantifies the method variance introduced by different models and prompts is often preferable to relying on a single model with a single prompt (Hussain et al., 2024). If only one or a few setups are tested, it remains unclear whether LLM performance generalizes to other materials and procedural variations, which raises the question of whether scientific knowledge has actually been generated (Argyle et al., 2025). Our simulation-based ADEMP framework complements other approaches which emphasize the importance of incrementally developing LLM methods for a specific task of interest (Conde et al., 2026). Besides rigorous method evaluation, the multiverse approach can also be useful for exploring the impact of different methodological factors, such as model type, hyperparameter settings, or prompt details. Once a strong configuration has been identified for a given task, subsequent evaluations can compare new models or prompting strategies against this best-performing configuration.

Due to the fully crossed design of a multiverse study, its computational costs are much higher than those of a single LLM setup, especially for large stimulus sets such as the norms of concreteness, valence, and arousal generated by Martínez et al. (2024) for 126,397 single words and 63,680 multi-word expressions. These costs can be limited by applying an ADEMP validation study to a random subset of stimuli from the target corpus. Because the subset is a random sample, the findings generalize to the remaining stimuli, with the item-based standard error quantifying the uncertainty of this generalization. The best-performing configuration can then be used to rate the full corpus, for which obtaining human ratings would be infeasible (e.g., Beucler et al., 2026; Martínez et al., 2024). Such validated LLM ratings offer a fast and cheap alternative to human ratings and can be used to sample stimuli representatively from the whole range of a construct for subsequent studies with human participants, as done by Martínez et al. (2024). However, stimulus sets that cover all areas of the response distribution equally, as in the present case study, may increase construct (universe score) variance and thereby lead to an overestimation of the generalizability coefficient.

We illustrated the new ADEMP template by conceptually replicating and extending the validation study by Martínez et al. (2024). In line with their findings, we observed high correlations between human and LLM ratings of valence and arousal.

However, with smaller local models, rating quality depended on the chosen model and, to a lesser extent, on the response format and prompt examples, particularly in combination, as quantified by the variance components (Brennan, 2001). A limitation is that subjective human ratings served as the benchmark, which need not be correct and can be distorted by inattentive responding and other response biases (e.g., Stosic et al., 2024). Given the high reliability of the human ratings and the difficulty of measuring valence and arousal otherwise, however, there seems to be no better alternative benchmark. Despite the sensitivity of LLM-generated ratings to methodological choices, even modestly sized, locally run open-weight models with approximately 8 to 27 billion parameters produced valence ratings that correlated with human ratings comparably to GPT-4o, particularly when ratings were averaged over repeated queries under identical conditions.

Concerning limitations, LLM performance may vary even for related constructs:

For arousal, open-weight models reached only adequate performance (r ≈ .80; see Results), below that of GPT-4o (Martínez et al., 2024). This may partly reflect properties of the construct, since arousal ratings are generally less consistent across norming studies than valence ratings (Muraki & Pexman, 2025; Warriner et al., 2013).

Alternatively, the paper and data by Martínez et al. (2024) may have been part of the training data of some models (e.g., gpt-oss and gemma3, published in 2025), which could inflate performance estimates ("leakage"; Feuerriegel et al., 2025; Hullman et al., 2026), possibly more so for valence than for arousal. Ruling out this explanation requires replicating the present investigation with new stimulus materials and human ratings.

Finally, other procedural details besides model type, prompt examples, and response scale may affect LLM response quality; while we selected those deemed most relevant, future research is required to study other prompt design choices (Fang et al., 2026).

A fundamental caveat concerns the interpretation of LLMs' predictive performance. While LLM output may show high correlations of up to .95 with human ratings, such high predictive performance does not imply that LLMs have a causal understanding of cognitive processes in humans or that the underlying mechanisms are equivalent (Demszky et al., 2023). Loru et al. (2025) investigated this question and showed that LLMs produced output similar to that of human raters in a news classification task, but humans and LLMs still differed in the processes leading to their conclusions. Furthermore, high correlations between LLM and human ratings do not justify simply replacing human participants with LLMs. Rather, systematic LLM simulations varying procedural details, planned and possibly preregistered with the ADEMP template, allow researchers to investigate where discrepancies between LLM and human ratings may occur and which factors are relevant for minimizing this gap.

When using commercial LLMs as a research tool, the lack of information about model architecture as well as training data and procedures threatens scientific transparency and reproducibility. Additionally, many large models cannot be run locally and are accessible exclusively through APIs (Feuerriegel et al., 2025; Wulff & Mata, 2025a). In the present study, we employed open-weight models run locally using Ollama (Ollama, 2026), accessed via ellmer in R (Wickham et al., 2025), thereby enabling other researchers to easily replicate and extend our analyses. When accessed via programming languages such as Python, open models even allow researchers to access internal model information such as log probabilities of LLM predictions (which reflect the uncertainty associated with each response) or to apply fine-tuning to further increase the correlation with human ratings (Hussain et al., 2024; Martínez et al., 2024). However, open-weights models are not without limitations. For instance, even if the architecture and weights are openly available, the complete set of factors, design choices, and training data relevant to their development may not be known.

Another general issue is the substantial computational and environmental cost of LLMs (Abdurahman et al., 2024; Debelak et al., 2025; Demszky et al., 2023), which can be mitigated by smaller models that run locally on consumer-level hardware. Costs also increase with the context length (i.e., the number of input and output words a model can consider; Hussain et al., 2024), and long inputs may be more difficult for LLMs to process (Huang et al., 2025). In the present investigation, we used concise rating instructions and requested only integer ratings, thus keeping context length minimal.

Finally, LLM output may be biased related to demographic factors such as race or sex. This is especially critical when using LLMs for rating tasks, as LLMs may replicate existing societal biases present in their training data (Abdurahman et al., 2025; Debelak et al., 2025; Guest et al., 2025). By conducting an LLM simulation study using the present framework, researchers can investigate biases. On the one hand, biases not specific to particular items will manifest as changes in the absolute level of all LLM ratings, and thus in a larger main effect of model type on stimulus ratings (e.g., generally higher ratings for one model than another model). On the other hand, model biases specific to certain item properties will manifest as an interaction between model and stimulus type (e.g., systematically different ratings for items involving men vs. women). 8For instance, researchers may systematically vary certain terms and content related to specific demographic groups in the stimulus materials (e.g., whether an applicant is framed as male or female) to examine how specific aspects affect LLM ratings.

The proposed template can also be used for more specialized and advanced methods of eliciting LLM ratings. For instance, researchers may forgo LLM prompting altogether and instead extract psychological constructs from text data using embedding spaces provided by certain models. Recent studies have used embedding spaces to analyze semantic relationships between various psychological constructs and item texts (e.g., Herderich et al., 2024; Hommel and Arslan, 2025; Hommel et al., 2026; Wulff and Mata, 2025b). Similarly, fine-tuning can tailor LLMs to specific tasks (Conde et al., 2026; Hussain et al., 2024). Although a multiverse of design choices is not strictly needed for continually improving a fine-tuned model, the ADEMP approach can help evaluate how the choice of base model and hyperparameter settings affects the resulting fine-tuned models.

In conclusion, the present paper contributes to the robust use of language models as a research tool by developing a workflow for evaluating LLM-generated ratings. We adapted the ADEMP template for statistical simulation studies to facilitate the planning and reporting of LLM simulations. The framework draws on generalizability theory to disentangle the contributions of items, model and prompt choices as well as repeated iterations to the consistency of LLM ratings (Brennan, 2001; Cronbach, 1972), while using inter-rater reliability with human ratings as a gold standard for validity (Goodwin, 2001). Overall, our framework provides a psychometric perspective on evaluating LLM output across the multiverse of arbitrary model and prompt choices.

Appendix A Prompt Examples

Each LLM prompt consists of five components that are concatenated in each iteration of the simulation: 1.

An explanation of the task, 2. the range of responses allowed, 3. examples for multi-word expressions, 4. the target multi-word expression to be rated, and 5. a reminder for the range of responses allowed.

The examples below are based on Prompt 2 provided by Martínez et al. (2024) for ratings of valence. Ratings of arousal were analogous modifications of Prompt 3 (not provided here).

Example prompt with examples of low and high valence (original version of Prompt 2 in Martínez et al.):

Could you please rate how reading the following multi-word expression makes a person feel. Use a scale from 1 to 9, where 1 means very negative, bad and 9 means very positive, good. Examples of words that would get a rating of 1 are pedophile, AIDS, and wreck. Examples of words that would get a rating of 9 are vacation, fantastic, and laugh.

The expression is: [insert expression here]. Only answer a number from 1 to 9. Please limit your answer to numbers.

Example prompt with only examples of low valence:

Could you please rate how reading the following multi-word expression makes a person feel. Use a scale from 1 to 9, where 1 means very negative, bad and 9 means very positive, good. Examples of words that would get a rating of 1 are pedophile, AIDS, and wreck. The expression is: [insert expression here]. Only answer a number from 1 to 9.

Please limit your answer to numbers. Examples for multi-word expressions are (taken from Martínez et al., 2024):

Appendix B Documentation of LLM Parameters

This section documents the parameter settings that were in effect when the models described in the paper were run locally using Ollama (version 0.12.9) and accessed via the R package ellmer (version 0.4.0). All LLM calls were run successively on a single GPU (RTX 5090, 32 GB VRAM). All statements refer to the source code of these versions; the online documentation of Ollama partly deviates from it (e.g., it lists a default context length of 2048 tokens).

Ollama determines the parameters of each request in three steps, with each step overriding the previous one: ( 1 When a request sent to this endpoint does not specify temperature or top-p, Ollama sets both to 1 and passes them on as request options (see function FromChatRequest() in https://github.com/ollama/ollama/blob/v0.12.9/openai/openai.go, lines 556-577).

Because request options take precedence, these values override both the Ollama defaults and the Modelfile parameters listed above. No other sampling parameters are set by default on this endpoint. In addition, Ollama increases the context length for the gpt-oss model family to at least 8192 tokens unless the total VRAM of the GPU is below 20 GiB (see function scheduleRunner() in https://github.com/ollama/ollama/blob/v0.12.9/server/routes.go), which did not apply to our GPU. Consequently, the parameters in effect in our simulation were: • temperature = 1 and top-p = 1 for all models • top-k = 64 for gemma3 (4b, 12b, 27b) and top-k = 40 for all other models • num_ctx = 8192 for gpt-oss (20b) and num_ctx = 4096 for all other models • all remaining parameters at the Ollama or Modelfile defaults listed above

The supplementary temperature analysis (20 iterations per condition with default settings and temperatures of 0.8 and 1.0) is consistent with these settings; ratings obtained with default settings corresponded to those obtained with a temperature of 1 rather than 0.8. Note that the documentation of ellmer 0.4.0 states that models accessed via Ollama "can only use 2048 input tokens". This note does not reflect the effective context length in our setup (see above). All prompts in our simulation were far shorter than 2048 tokens, so that none of the context limits affected the input. The gpt-oss override further illustrates that effective settings can deviate from documented defaults and should be verified in the source code or empirically. No reasoning effort was specified, so gpt-oss (20b) ran at its default reasoning level.

All other invalid values resulted from violations of the requested response format: gemma3 (4b): 2; gemma3 (12b, 27b): 0; llama3.1 (8b): 263; phi3 (3.8b): 2,216; phi3 (14b): 43; phi4 (14b): 40; gpt-oss (20b): 82. These values were more frequent with the 0-100 scale (N = 2, 451) than with the 1-9 scale (N = 195), suggesting that the finer 100-point format is harder for LLMs to adhere to. By example type, there were 671 (none), 230 (low only), 805 (high only), and 940 (both) invalid values. Overall, missing or invalid values made up only 0.44% of all valence ratings (arousal: 0.06%; see supplementary materials). No condition exceeded 20% missing or invalid values.
